samples.guide: Use familiar concrete words, explicit subjects, one idea per clause and clear repetition. Use correct agreement, tense and aspect; honor regional preferences without assuming Chilean Spanish.
samples.brief: Two friends at a railway station discover their tickets are for different destinations.

content.title: Dos boletos diferentes
content.story:
Ana y Luis están en la estación. Ana tiene una mochila. Luis tiene los boletos.

Un tren está frente a Ana y Luis.

—El tren va a Santiago —dice Ana—. ¿Tienes mi boleto?

—Sí. Aquí tienes —dice Luis.

Ana mira su boleto. El boleto dice: «Destino: Santiago».

—Tengo un boleto para Santiago —dice Ana—. ¿Tú también?

Luis mira su boleto.

—No. Mi boleto dice: «Destino: Talca».

Ana mira el boleto de Luis. Después, Ana mira su boleto otra vez.

—Tú tienes un boleto para Talca. Yo tengo un boleto para Santiago —dice Ana.

—Sí. Los destinos son diferentes —dice Luis—. No tenemos boletos para el mismo tren.

Ana y Luis no suben al tren. Luis tiene los dos boletos en la mano. Ana ve una oficina cerca.

—Podemos preguntar allí —dice Ana.

content.title: Dos billetes diferentes
content.story:
Ana y Luis están en la estación. Ana tiene una bolsa. Luis tiene una mochila. Los dos amigos quieren viajar a Madrid.

—Yo tengo mi billete —dice Ana.

—Yo también tengo mi billete —dice Luis.

Ana mira su billete.

—Mi tren sale a las diez. ¿Y tu tren?

Luis revisa su billete. Luis mira la hora.

—Mi tren también sale a las diez.

Ana mira el billete de Luis. Ana ve un nombre: Toledo.

—Luis, ¿tu destino es Toledo?

—No, mi destino es Madrid.

—Pero tu billete dice «Toledo».

Luis mira su billete otra vez.

—Sí, es verdad. Mi billete es para Toledo. ¿Tu billete es para Madrid?

Ana muestra su billete.

—Sí. Mira: Madrid.

Los dos amigos miran los billetes.

—Tenemos dos billetes para dos destinos diferentes —dice Luis.

—Sí —dice Ana—. No podemos viajar juntos con estos billetes.

Luis ve una ventanilla. Una mujer está detrás de la ventanilla.

—Podemos preguntar allí —dice Luis.

Ana toma su bolsa. Los dos amigos caminan hacia la ventanilla.

glossary.meaning: And; connects people or ideas. In ¿Y tu tren?, it means “And your train?”
To be in a place. Están is used for Ana and Luis together; está is used for one woman.
In or at; en la estación means “at the station.”
The. El and la accompany singular nouns; los accompanies masculine plural nouns.
Station; here, a railway station.
To have. Tiene means “has”; tengo means “I have”; Tenemos means “we have.”
A or an. Una accompanies feminine nouns; un accompanies masculine nouns.
Bag; the bag Ana carries.
Backpack; the bag Luis carries on his back.
Two. Los dos amigos means “the two friends” or “both friends.”
Friend. Amigos is plural and refers to Ana and Luis together.
To want. Quieren means “they want” and is followed here by viajar.
To travel. This infinitive follows verbs meaning “want” or “can.”
To; introduces the destination in viajar a Madrid.
I; the person speaking.
My; shows that the ticket or train belongs to the speaker. Mi is capitalized at the start of a sentence.
Ticket; here, a train ticket. Billetes is plural.
To say. Dice means “says”; a ticket dice a place name when that name is written on it.
Also or too; adds something that is true for the other friend as well.
To look at. Mira means “looks at,” while miran means “they look at.” Mira in Ana's dialogue is a command: “Look.”
His or her here; su billete refers to the ticket belonging to the person named.
Train.
To leave or depart. Sale means “departs,” describing a train's departure time.
At ten o'clock. A las introduces the time of an event.
Ten; here, ten o'clock.
Your; refers to something belonging to the person being spoken to. It has no accent.
To check or examine. Revisa means “checks,” here by reading a ticket.
Time; here, the departure time printed on the ticket.
Of; in el billete de Luis, it shows that the ticket belongs to Luis.
To see or notice. Ve means “sees,” here noticing a name or a ticket window.
Name; here, the name of the destination printed on the ticket.
Destination; the place a journey leads to. Destinos is plural.
To be; identifies a destination or what a ticket is for. Es means “is.”
No or not. No answers a question negatively; before podemos, it means “not.”
But; introduces information that contrasts with what Luis says.
Again; Luis looks at his ticket a second time.
Yes; an affirmative answer. The accent distinguishes it from si, meaning “if.”
It is true; here, an acknowledgment that Ana is right.
For or to; identifies the destination a ticket is valid for.
To show. Muestra means “shows”; Ana lets Luis see her ticket.
Different; not the same. Diferentes is plural to agree with destinos.
To be able to or can. Podemos means “we can”; No podemos means “we cannot.” It is followed by an infinitive.
Together. Juntos has a plural ending because it refers to both friends.
With; here, using the tickets they have.
This. Estos means “these” and agrees with the masculine plural billetes.
Ticket window or service counter at the station.
Woman; here, the woman behind the ticket window.
Behind; describes the woman's position relative to the ticket window.
To ask; here, to ask the woman for information or help.
There; refers to the ticket window they can see.
To take or pick up. Toma means “picks up,” describing Ana taking her bag.
To walk. Caminan means “they walk.”
Toward; indicates the direction the friends walk.

materialIssues: «No tenemos boletos para el mismo tren.» — Different ticket destinations do not necessarily imply different trains: one train can serve multiple destinations. The scene needs another detail to justify this conclusion.
«Luis tiene los dos boletos en la mano.» — Ana has been examining her ticket, but its return to Luis is not narrated, creating a small continuity gap.
«Podemos preguntar allí» — The modal-plus-infinitive construction and location reference lack definitions. Along with several other omissions, this materially limits the requested broad support.
strengths: Short present-tense clauses, explicit names and repeated destinations suit the supplied A1 guide.
All supplied definitions are contextually sound; the boarding sense of subir is particularly useful.
Boleto is a legitimate regional choice without requiring an assumption of Chilean Spanish.
The office offers a clear next step while leaving the ticket problem naturally unresolved.

materialIssues: «My; shows that the ticket or train belongs to the speaker.» — Accurate for possession of the ticket, but mi tren means the train the speaker plans to take, not a train they own. The definition should distinguish association from ownership.

«No podemos viajar juntos con estos billetes.» — This combines negation, a modal plus infinitive, an agreeing together-expression and a demonstrative noun phrase. It is a relative load increase within this A1 scene, although the notes explain its components well.
strengths: The shared intention to visit Madrid makes Luis's Toledo ticket a clear problem, without assuming different destinations necessarily mean different trains.
The discovery proceeds coherently from departure times to the printed destination and then toward help.
